h1: ACGME Compliance Checker for Multi-Department GME
paragraph: A checker tells you what is already wrong. We build the schedule with your program's requirements in it from the start, so there is far less to find afterwards.

cta.title: Hand Over the Build
cta.description: Join 30+ departments across 20+ hospitals and practices who rely on Scheduling Wizard for ACGME-compliant schedules. Finished schedules in your format, with redrafts through the year included.

faq.question: Is Scheduling Wizard an ACGME compliance checker?
faq.answer: No, and it is worth being direct about that. A compliance checker audits a schedule you already built and reports what breaks. We do the building. Your program's ACGME requirements go in while the schedule is created, which is a different job and makes most of the checking unnecessary. If what you specifically want is a tool that audits an existing schedule, a residency management platform like New Innovations or MedHub is closer to what you are after.

An ACGME compliance checker is a tool that verifies whether an existing residency or fellowship schedule meets the duty hour requirements. It is useful, and it is a different job from ours. We build the schedule with those requirements already in it, so what comes back has far less to check. Programs that want an audit tool as well usually get it from their residency management platform.
faq.question: What is an ACGME compliance checker and how does it work?

faq.answer: Our team has subspecialty-specific ACGME rule knowledge built in. This matters because ACGME requirements differ across program types, and a generic compliance checker that applies universal rules will miss the subspecialty requirements that differ from one program to the next. When you engage Scheduling Wizard, your program's specific duty hour rules are modeled into the schedule itself before any schedule is generated.
faq.question: How does Scheduling Wizard handle subspecialty-specific ACGME rules?

faq.answer: The core standards: the 80-hour weekly limit averaged over four weeks, eight hours off between duty periods, 14 hours free after 24-hour in-house call, the 24-hour cap on continuous duty with up to four hours for transitions, one day off in seven averaged over four weeks, and the home call rules. On top of those, the specialty-specific Program Requirements for your program. We work from the requirements your program tells us apply, and we redraft when something needs to change.
faq.question: Which ACGME duty hour rules does our team work from?

faq.answer: No. Scheduling Wizard operates as a managed service, not a self-service software platform. There is no client-facing tool to learn or operate. You submit your program's rules, and Scheduling Wizard delivers finished, ACGME-compliant schedules as ready-to-use Excel spreadsheets that your team can upload directly to your existing publishing platform.
faq.question: Do I need to learn scheduling software to use this service?

faq.answer: Scheduling Wizard handles scheduling across multiple departments simultaneously, applying the correct ACGME compliance rules for each program individually. GME offices can rely on a consistent compliance process across their entire hospital system rather than managing separate manual auditing workflows for each department. Currently, Scheduling Wizard serves 30+ departments across 20+ hospitals and practices.
faq.question: How does Scheduling Wizard support GME offices managing multiple programs?

faq.answer: With manual scheduling, ACGME rule knowledge and scheduling logic often leave with outgoing chiefs. Scheduling Wizard retains your program's rule configurations and ACGME rule modeling year over year, so incoming chief residents inherit a fully configured, compliant scheduling system rather than starting the compliance process from scratch each academic year.
faq.question: What happens to ACGME compliance knowledge when chief residents change?

A program coordinator seeking a complete solution to confirm that all rotations and call schedules are compliant with ACGME requirements, worried about the legal and operational risks of non-compliance.

A GME office administrator looking for a method to regularly audit the scheduling process across multiple departments to maintain ACGME compliance, understanding that generic software won’t cater to specific subspecialty rules.
